lead: Two ideas from engine history are back in the exam: the stratified charge engine and the low heat rejection (LHR) engine. A stratified charge engine places an easy-to-ignite rich mixture at the spark plug and a lean mixture everywhere else, so a spark-ignition engine can run lean overall and control its load without a throttle. An LHR engine insulates the combustion chamber so less heat leaks to the coolant. Both aim at efficiency; each pays for it in emissions or reliability.
prereq: You need: carburettor mixture limits, gasoline direct injection (Fuel supply and ignition systems), and engine heat balance (Engine testing and performance).

blocks.text: A homogeneous petrol mixture can be lit by a spark only between about φ = 0.7 and 1.3. To give part load, a normal petrol engine therefore keeps the mixture near stoichiometric and lowers the amount of it with a throttle. The throttle makes the piston pull against a partial vacuum on every intake stroke: this pumping loss is why petrol engines are inefficient at light load.

A stratified charge is deliberately non-uniform: rich (φ about 1 to 1.3) at the plug, very lean or even pure air elsewhere. The spark lights the rich zone easily, and its flame burns into the lean rest. Load is then controlled by the amount of fuel, as in a diesel (quality control), with the throttle wide open. The overall air–fuel ratio can be 20 to 40 or more. The gains:

items: Less pumping loss, because the throttle stays open.
A higher ratio of specific heats in the lean charge and less heat loss from the cooler gas near the walls, so a higher cycle efficiency.
Less tendency to knock in the lean end gas, so a higher compression ratio is possible.
Low CO, since oxygen is plentiful.

blocks.text: Divided-chamber (pre-chamber) engines. A small pre-chamber in the head, holding the spark plug, gets a rich mixture; the main chamber gets a lean one. In the Honda CVCC (compound vortex controlled combustion) engine of the 1970s a third, small intake valve fed the pre-chamber from a separate carburettor circuit. The burning rich mixture shoots out as flame jets, a torch, and burns the lean main charge. The CVCC met the strict US emission rules of 1975 without a catalytic converter. Modern racing and some production engines use a similar pre-chamber jet ignition.

Open-chamber, direct-injection engines. Fuel is injected straight into the cylinder late in compression so that a rich cloud reaches the plug at the moment of the spark. The Texaco controlled combustion system (TCCS) and Ford PROCO used strong swirl to carry the spray past the plug. Modern gasoline direct injection (GDI) does it three ways: wall-guided, a shaped piston bowl deflects the spray to the plug; air-guided, tumble or swirl carries it; spray-guided, a precise piezo injector places the spray edge right at the plug. At high load these engines switch to a homogeneous λ = 1 charge for full power.

The costs: HC rises from the over-lean edges of the cloud, soot can form in the richest zone around the injector, the spark plug can foul, and, above all, a lean exhaust cannot use a three-way catalyst for NOx. Stratified GDI cars therefore needed a lean NOx trap and low-sulphur fuel; when particle and NOx limits tightened, most makers went back to λ = 1 direct injection.

About a quarter to a third of the fuel energy in a diesel goes into the coolant. An LHR engine (also called an insulated or, in its extreme form, an “adiabatic” engine) reduces this by insulating the surfaces the hot gas touches: piston crown, cylinder head, valve faces and liner top. The usual method is a thermal barrier coating, typically 0.3 to 0.5 mm of yttria-stabilised zirconia (a ceramic of low conductivity, about 1 to 2 W/(m·K)) sprayed on a metallic bond coat. Other methods are ceramic inserts and air-gap pistons, which trap an insulating layer of air under a separate crown.

The expected gain is smaller than it looks. Heat kept from the coolant mostly leaves with the exhaust, not as piston work, so the extra brake efficiency is a few per cent at best unless the hot exhaust drives a turbocharger or a turbo-compound turbine. The hot walls also heat the incoming air, lowering volumetric efficiency, and raise the gas temperature, which raises NOx. The lubricating oil on the liner breaks down above about 250 °C, which limits how hot the walls may run.

LHR suits the diesel, which likes hot walls: the ignition delay shortens and diesel knock falls, and low-cetane fuels such as alcohols and vegetable oils ignite more easily. It does not suit the petrol engine, where hot walls cause knock.

blocks.where: ΔT is the temperature drop across the coating in K; q the heat flux through it in W/m²; t its thickness in m; k its thermal conductivity in W/(m·K).

examples.question: In a divided-chamber engine each cycle puts 0.05 g of air with fuel at an air–fuel ratio of 12 into the pre-chamber and 0.50 g of air at an air–fuel ratio of 22 into the main chamber. Find the fuel in each chamber, the overall air–fuel ratio and λ (stoichiometric 14.7).
examples.answer: The charge is lean overall, air–fuel ratio 20.4 (λ = 1.39), while the plug fires a rich mixture at λ = 0.82.

examples.question: A 1.5 L four-stroke petrol engine at 2000 rev/min gives 15 kW at part load. Throttled, the intake manifold is at 0.50 bar and the exhaust at 1.05 bar; run stratified and unthrottled, the intake is at 0.95 bar. Estimate the pumping power each way and the saving as a share of the output.
steps: Pumping work per cycle ≈ (p<sub>exhaust</sub> − p<sub>intake</sub>) × swept volume.
Throttled: (1.05 − 0.50) × 10⁵ Pa × 1.5 × 10⁻³ m³ = 82.5 J per cycle.
A four-stroke engine completes one cycle every two revolutions: 2000 ÷ 120 = 16.7 cycles per second.
Pumping power: 82.5 × 16.7 = 1375 W throttled; 15.0 × 16.7 = 250 W unthrottled.
Saving: 1375 − 250 = 1125 W, that is 1.125 ÷ 15 = 7.5 % of the output.
examples.answer: Removing the throttle saves about 1.1 kW of pumping power, 7.5 % of the 15 kW output, before any gain from the lean cycle itself.

examples.question: A piston crown carries a mean heat flux of 0.5 MW/m². Find the temperature drop across (a) a 0.5 mm zirconia coating with k = 1.0 W/(m·K) and (b) 10 mm of aluminium crown with k = 150 W/(m·K), for the same flux.
steps: A layer 20 times thinner holds almost eight times the temperature drop, because its conductivity is 150 times lower.
examples.answer: The coating holds about 250 K and the metal only 33 K, so the coated surface runs much hotter and less heat passes; in practice the flux itself falls too, so this is a first estimate.

traps: Saying a stratified charge engine runs a rich mixture: it is rich only at the plug; overall it is lean.
Fitting only a three-way catalyst to a stratified lean engine: NOx needs a lean NOx trap or SCR.
Expecting the coolant heat saved by an LHR engine to appear as brake power: most of it leaves in the exhaust unless it is recovered.
Recommending LHR for a petrol engine: hot walls cause knock; LHR helps the diesel.
Forgetting that hot LHR walls raise NOx and lower volumetric efficiency.

quiz.a: A charge whose mixture strength varies through the chamber: rich at the spark plug, lean elsewhere, lean overall.

quiz.q: Name the coating material most used in LHR engines and its usual thickness.
quiz.a: Yttria-stabilised zirconia, about 0.3 to 0.5 mm, on a metallic bond coat.

quiz.q: How does a stratified charge engine control load, and why does that save fuel?
quiz.a: By the amount of fuel injected, with the throttle open (quality control). The open throttle removes most of the pumping loss of a throttled engine at part load.

quiz.q: Why does an LHR engine raise NOx?
quiz.a: Insulated walls keep the gas hotter during combustion, and thermal NO rises steeply with peak temperature.

quiz.q: A pre-chamber holds 0.04 g air at an air–fuel ratio of 12; the main chamber 0.40 g air at 25. Find the overall λ.
Find the temperature drop across a 0.3 mm coating of k = 1.2 W/(m·K) at 0.6 MW/m².
Explain why LHR engines gave much smaller efficiency gains than the coolant heat they saved suggested.
quiz.a: Most of the saved heat stays in the gas and leaves with the exhaust; only a small part becomes piston work. Hot walls also heat the intake air, lowering volumetric efficiency, and the oil limits wall temperature. A turbo-compound turbine is needed to recover the extra exhaust energy.

beyond: Not for the exam. Pre-chamber jet ignition, first proved in motor racing, is now used in some production petrol engines to burn very lean or heavily diluted charges. Thermal barrier coatings return in a new form, thin “temperature-swing” coatings that heat and cool within each cycle so the intake air is not warmed. Search next for “turbulent jet ignition”, “spray-guided GDI” and “temperature swing coating”.

figure.caption: A divided-chamber stratified charge engine, the CVCC type. A small valve fills the pre-chamber with a rich mixture that the plug lights easily; jets of flame then burn the lean main charge. With the worked example’s masses the whole charge is lean, λ = 1.39, while the plug still sees an air–fuel ratio of 12.

spec.aria: Cross-section of a cylinder with a small pre-chamber in the head. The pre-chamber has its own small valve, a spark plug and a rich mixture at air-fuel ratio 12; three flame jets pass through a nozzle into the main chamber, which holds a lean mixture at 22. A side panel gives 0.05 grams of air in the pre-chamber, 0.50 in the main chamber, and an overall ratio of 20.4, lambda 1.39.
